Chapter 8: The Toll of Touring and the Fragility of Health
Touring. A lot of people picture it as this endless adventure—freedom on the open road, every night a new city, a new crowd, a new story. Sounds pretty incredible, right? But, honestly, the reality is way more complicated.
There’s a rhythm you fall into when you’re on tour: those long hours in a van or a cramped bus, the frantic set-up during sound checks, grabbing food on the fly, and then—boom—the energy spike of the show. At first, it’s a rush. Seeing new places, meeting new faces—it feels like you’re living the dream. But after a while, the cracks start to show.
Sleep? That becomes a rare luxury, and your body starts to feel every mile you’ve traveled. Colds just stick around, injuries get ignored, and suddenly, it’s hard to tell where self-care ends and self-destruction begins.
Picture this: after a string of back-to-back shows, one of the band members suddenly collapses backstage. The room just freezes. In that moment, you can almost hear everyone thinking the same thing—this life is more fragile than we want to admit. There’s a mad rush to the hospital, phones blowing up, and a heavy, sobering realization that something has to give. That incident? It’s a wake-up call. It makes you see—none of us can outrun the limits of our own bodies, no matter how determined our minds are.
And it’s not just the physical strain that wears you down. Mental health is always on a knife’s edge. The rush of performing can be intoxicating, but it’s always followed by the lows—loneliness, anxiety, that gnawing pressure to keep going and never show weakness. There are nights filled with worry, staring at the ceiling, wondering if everything could fall apart at any moment.
Over time, the band starts to notice these patterns. They begin to watch out for one another, learning to spot the signs of burnout and actually reaching out when someone’s struggling. Conversations shift—they talk about setting boundaries, why rest matters, and that sometimes, it’s okay to ask for help. Of course, it’s not always smooth. Old habits are tough to break, and let’s be real—the music world often rewards those who push themselves to the brink. But, slowly, things start to change.
Most people only see the glamorous side of touring: the lights, the crowds, the excitement. What they don’t see is the price you pay behind the scenes. For folks actually living on the road, the real challenge is survival—finding ways to care for yourself and the people around you, even when the world keeps asking for more than you have to give.
